title: Stargazing in Namibia Works Best Around the New Moon, So Plan Your Astronomy Club's Trip From There
meta_title: Stargazing in Namibia for Astronomy Clubs and Groups
meta_description: Stargazing in Namibia for astronomy groups: the best months, dark sky lodges, astronomy farms and how to time your club's trip to the new moon.
excerpt: Stargazing in Namibia is world class. Here is how astronomy clubs pick the month, the dark-sky lodges and the route for a private group trip.
content:
Stargazing in Namibia is about as good as it gets on Earth: dry desert air, high plateaus and almost no artificial light give skies dark enough for the Milky Way to cast a faint glow. For astronomy groups, the best plan is a private trip in the dry winter, timed around the new moon.

Organising a club trip means more than finding dark skies. You need lodges with observing space, guides who can run a telescope session for 12 people, and a route that does not leave members exhausted before the sun goes down. This guide covers when to go, where to stay, what you will see and how we set up club safaris for astronomy societies.

Quick Facts

  • Best months: May to September, the dry winter, is the peak for stargazing in Namibia; aim within about four nights of the new moon
  • Darkest protected sky: For stargazing in Namibia, the darkest protected site is NamibRand Nature Reserve, an International Dark Sky Reserve (Gold tier) since 2012
  • Astronomy farms: Hakos Astrofarm area near the Gamsberg, about 1,850 m above sea level
  • Ideal group size: 6 to 16 people in two or three vehicles
  • Trip length: 7 to 10 days, with at least four nights at dark-sky stops
  • Night temperatures: Close to freezing in June and July on the highlands and in the desert
  • Getting there: Fly into Windhoek (Hosea Kutako International Airport), then travel by road or light aircraft

Why Is Stargazing in Namibia So Good?

Stargazing in Namibia benefits from three things at once: very dry air, high altitude and one of the lowest population densities in the world. Cloud-free nights are common for much of the year, and stargazing in Namibia happens across huge areas with no towns, no street lights and no glow on the horizon.

The Namib Desert and the central highlands also sit close to the Tropic of Capricorn. From here, the richest part of the southern sky, including the centre of our galaxy, passes almost straight overhead. Northern-hemisphere astronomers see objects that never rise at home, and see them high, clear of the haze that sits near the horizon.

NamibRand: Africa's first dark sky reserve

The NamibRand Nature Reserve, a private reserve of roughly 215,000 hectares on the eastern edge of the Namib-Naukluft National Park, was named an International Dark Sky Reserve in May 2012. According to the NamibRand dark sky page, it holds Gold tier status, the darkest and strictest category, and was the first such reserve in Africa.

That status comes with rules. Outdoor light fittings in the reserve follow dark-sky standards, there are limits on how bright fixtures may be, and even vehicle headlights are covered by guidelines. A sky quality meter on the reserve office roof records the darkness every five minutes through the night. For a group, it means stargazing in Namibia's darkest reserve is protected rather than left to luck.

Altitude, dry air and empty land

Away from NamibRand, the inland plateau around the Gamsberg and the Khomas Highland is the other great region for stargazing in Namibia. The H.E.S.S. gamma-ray observatory, run by an international research collaboration, sits about 100 km south-west of Windhoek at 1,800 m for exactly this reason, and amateur observatories cluster on guest farms in the same area.

When Is the Best Time for Stargazing in Namibia?

The best time for stargazing in Namibia is the dry winter from May to September, when rain is rare and nights are crisp and clear. Within any month, the new moon matters even more than the season: plan the darkest-sky nights of your trip for the days around it.

For stargazing in Namibia, summer is the harder season. Summer (roughly November to March) brings the rains to central and northern Namibia. Afternoon thunderstorms often clear by night, and the south-west stays drier, but you lose more nights to cloud and humidity. Winter is cold after dark, yet that is a small price for night after night of steady, transparent sky.

Plan the route around the new moon

A bright moon washes out faint galaxies and nebulae for days on either side of full. We build each astronomy itinerary so that the two or three nights at the darkest site fall within a few days of the new moon, with the travel and sightseeing days placed at the brighter end of the cycle. Moon phase shapes stargazing in Namibia more than any lodge choice. Look up the phase for your chosen month before you fix flights, because a week's shift can double the number of truly dark hours.

For more on rainfall, heat and wildlife by month, read our guide to the best time to visit Namibia.

Where Should an Astronomy Group Stay?

Astronomy groups get the most from stargazing in Namibia by splitting their nights between two kinds of base: a desert lodge in or near NamibRand for wide, dark skies and the dunes of Sossusvlei, and an astronomy guest farm in the highlands for telescope time. Add a wildlife stop at the end if members want Etosha.

NamibRand and the Sossusvlei side

Wolwedans, a group of camps inside the NamibRand reserve, runs Dune Camp, Desert Lodge, Plains Camp, Boulders Camp and the Mountain View Suite. Small camps like these suit a society of 8 to 12 who want silence, star beds or open decks, and daytime access to the red dunes. The Namib-Naukluft park, with Sossusvlei and Deadvlei, lies next door, so the group gets the classic dune sunrise as well as the sky.

Our 3-day Namib Desert and Sossusvlei experience is a good short base to extend into a dark-sky stay focused on stargazing in Namibia's desert.

Hakos and the Gamsberg astronomy farms

The Gamsberg area south-west of Windhoek is the home of serious stargazing in Namibia and of the country's amateur astronomy scene. At Hakos Astrofarm, a German amateur society runs the IAS observatory at Hakos at about 1,852 m, with several large telescopes in domes and piers for visitors' own instruments. The family-run guest farm alongside hosts astronomers and offers guided stargazing.

Time on the larger instruments is normally arranged directly with the observatory operators, so serious imagers in your group should ask early. Casual members will be happy with a guided session through a farm telescope and good binoculars.

Places that are poor for stars

Not every famous stop works for stargazing in Namibia. Swakopmund and the coast are often wrapped in fog at night, and the main Etosha rest camps light up their waterholes for game viewing, which is wonderful for rhino but not for faint galaxies. Keep those for the daytime parts of the trip and save your observing for the desert and the highlands.

What Will Your Group See in the Southern Sky?

On a trip built for stargazing in Namibia, your group will see the southern sky at its best: the bright centre of the Milky Way, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, the Southern Cross and some of the finest star clusters in the sky, many of them invisible from Europe or North America.

In the winter months, Scorpius and Sagittarius ride high in the evening, and the dust lanes of the galactic centre are clear to the naked eye. Binoculars pick out the open clusters M6 and M7 near the scorpion's tail. Later in the night, or in the summer months, the Magellanic Clouds swing higher and the region around Carina and Crux comes into its own, with the Eta Carinae nebula and the globular cluster Omega Centauri as group favourites.

Stargazing in Namibia for beginners in the group

Most clubs mix keen observers with partners and friends who simply want to see the sky. Plan one relaxed session early in the trip with a guide pointing out the constellations by laser or red torch, before the dedicated observers head to the telescopes. Mixed groups enjoy stargazing in Namibia far more when nobody feels left out in the dark.

Astrophotographers should also read our Namibia photography tour guide for camera clubs, which covers dawn light in Deadvlei and planning shoots around the dunes.

How Do You Run a Group Stargazing Trip?

Group stargazing in Namibia runs on simple logistics: small vehicles, short driving days, lodges booked as a block and a guide who understands that the group's working day starts after dinner. The aim is to arrive at each dark-sky stop rested, with time to set up before nightfall.

Group size, vehicles and rooming

For stargazing in Namibia, groups of 6 to 16 work best. We put six or seven people in each 4x4 or safari vehicle so everyone has a window and space for camera bags, and a larger club travels as two or three vehicles in convoy. Twin rooms keep costs down, while members who will be up imaging at 3am often prefer a single room so they do not wake a roommate.

How group pricing works

Your per-person price depends on lodge level, season, group size and how you travel between regions. Vehicle and guide costs are shared, so they fall per person as the group grows, while lodge rates and park fees stay per person. Flying between regions by light aircraft saves long gravel days but costs more; road transfers are the budget choice. Ask us for a costed quote rather than relying on a headline price.

A sample 8-day astronomy route

4-6NamibRand or the Sossusvlei sideDunes and Deadvlei by day; three dark nights timed for the new moon

Insider Tips

  • Red light only: Give every member a red torch and agree no white light or phone screens near the telescopes
  • Dark adaptation: Allow 20 to 30 minutes for eyes to adjust before judging the sky
  • Warm layers: Down jacket, hat, gloves and a blanket for long winter sessions
  • Binoculars: A pair of 8x42 or 10x50 binoculars each is the best value kit for any member
  • Power: Bring spare batteries and check airline rules for lithium batteries before you fly
  • Nap time: Build a quiet afternoon into every observing day so people stay sharp after midnight

Why a Private Group Beats Joining a Mixed Tour

For stargazing in Namibia, a private group trip lets your club set the pace around the sky rather than around strangers. On a mixed tour, the observers who want to stay out until 2am are at odds with guests who need an early start, and nobody controls whether the itinerary lands on the new moon.

With your own trip, the organiser chooses the dates, the lodges and how many nights to spend at each dark site. Members share vehicles with people they know, talks and image reviews fit around dinner, and a single contact handles payments and changes. Frequently Asked Questions

Is Namibia good for stargazing?

Yes. Namibia is one of the best countries in the world for stargazing because of its dry desert air, high inland plateaus and very low population. The NamibRand Nature Reserve became Africa's first International Dark Sky Reserve in 2012, with Gold tier status, and astronomers have built private observatories on guest farms near the Gamsberg for decades.

When is the best month for stargazing in Namibia?

The best months for stargazing in Namibia are May to September, the dry winter, when skies are clearest and the centre of the Milky Way passes high overhead in the evening. Pick dates within a few nights of the new moon. October and April are good shoulder months, while January to March bring more storm cloud.

Do we need our own telescope for a Namibia stargazing trip?

No. Most groups do well with good binoculars, and astronomy guest farms and some desert lodges run guided sessions with their own telescopes. Serious observers can arrange time on larger instruments through the observatory operators in advance. If members bring their own kit, check airline rules for batteries and keep tripods in hold luggage.

How many people can join a group stargazing tour in Namibia?

Group stargazing tours in Namibia work best for 6 to 16 people. That fits two or three vehicles, keeps everyone close to the telescope during guided sessions and suits the small lodges and guest farms of the desert. Larger clubs can split into two parties on the same route a night apart.

How cold does it get at night on a winter stargazing trip?

Winter nights in the Namibian desert and on the highland farms can drop close to freezing, even after warm days in the mid-20s Celsius. Anyone stargazing in Namibia between May and August needs a warm jacket, hat, gloves and thick socks, plus a flask of something hot for long sessions outside.

Final Thoughts

Stargazing in Namibia rewards groups who plan around two things: the dry winter months and the new moon. Split your nights between a protected desert sky such as NamibRand and an astronomy farm near the Gamsberg, keep the driving days short, and your club will come home with the best skies of their lives.
